story.hook: Our Wedding Vendor Doubled the Price Overnight
story.script: My sister asked me to help organize her wedding because she hated negotiating and I kept spreadsheets for everything. Three months before the ceremony, we found a small event company that offered chairs, tables, lights, and a simple flower arch for one package price. The owner walked through the venue with us, counted every table, took photos of the loading entrance, and sent a detailed quote that evening. It included delivery, setup, collection, and tax. My sister paid the required deposit, and the owner emailed back saying our date and package were confirmed. I saved the quote, the invoice, the payment receipt, and every message in one folder. Two weeks before the wedding, the owner called my sister and said material costs had suddenly increased. He claimed the original quote covered only basic delivery and that setup would now cost extra. The new total was almost double. My sister panicked because every other vendor was already booked, and he knew we could not easily replace him. I asked him to email the revised amount and explain which contract clause allowed it. Instead, he sent a short message saying prices were subject to change and demanded the balance within twenty-four hours. I replied with his original invoice, where the words delivery and full setup appeared on three separate lines. He said that invoice was only an estimate. I sent back the receipt labeled final package deposit and his confirmation that the package price was locked. He stopped answering me and called my sister again. He told her I was making the process difficult and warned that arguing could risk a late setup on the wedding day. That threat changed everything. The venue manager had recommended his company, so I forwarded the complete email chain to her and asked whether vendors were allowed to threaten delayed service after taking a deposit. She called me ten minutes later. Apparently, his company had a preferred-vendor agreement with the venue, and one condition was honoring written quotes. The manager asked for permission to contact him. I said yes. That afternoon, the owner finally emailed us. He said there had been a misunderstanding and offered to keep the original price if we removed the flower arch. I forwarded that message too, because the arch was clearly included in the signed package. The venue manager then copied the regional events director into the conversation. The director explained that the company handled rentals for four properties in their group and that all four agreements were up for review the next month. She asked the owner to confirm, in writing, whether his business intended to ignore a paid invoice. His response arrived six minutes later. Suddenly the original package price was correct, setup was included, the flower arch was included, and there would be no delay. He even offered upgraded table linens at no charge. We accepted the written confirmation but declined the upgrade because we did not want another surprise condition. On the wedding morning, I arrived early with printed copies of every document. The trucks came on time. The chairs, tables, lights, and arch matched the order exactly. The owner supervised the setup himself and would barely look at me. Before he left, he asked whether I could tell the venue that everything had been resolved. I said I would tell them exactly what happened, including the part where he fixed it after they contacted him. My sister's wedding was beautiful, and she never had to pay one dollar above the original invoice. A month later, the venue manager told me they had renewed their rental agreements with a different company. The owner tried to double one wedding bill because he thought the date gave him leverage. Instead, his own written quote cost him four venues.

youtube.description: A vendor tried to change a confirmed wedding price. His own paperwork changed the ending.
